text.tspan: left: the line that ran · right: what the two sequences look like now
Two rules combined before the decoder ever sees them
The decoder has to ignore padding AND avoid reading ahead. This function turns both rules into a single tensor, so
never knows there were two. The frames run both builders and then the AND — the exact line where the two sentences stop being treated the same.

text.tspan: Teacher forcing cuts one tensor two ways: what the decoder reads, and what it must produce, shifted by one position.
Everything on this page runs on the first cut —
is why the decoder needs a mask that handles padding and word order at the same time. Read a column of the panel from top
to bottom and it says "given this, produce that":
separate training questions from one sentence, all answered in one forward pass — the whole
reason teacher forcing exists, and the reason a causal mask has to exist alongside it.

text.tspan: In this version the decoder uses the SAME embedding table as the encoder — one
— and the same positional encoding, so a token and a position mean exactly
the same thing on both sides of the model (
). After this line the target is lists of decimal numbers, and
embeddings are zero, the position signal added to them makes them look like any
other row — which is why the mask was built two frames ago.
Self-attention over the target: the text so far, compared with itself — using h, a normalised copy of x. The class
is the same as the encoder’s, and so are the lines inside it — only the mask differs, and that one difference
turns "read the whole sentence" into "read only what has been written so far". This is the first of three parts of a
; cross-attention and the feed-forward block follow, each with its own residual connection and
projections — the decoder does not share the encoder’s attention weights —
each. Nothing here knows about masking; the split is the same
